s: The medina's one true stage, day and night
w: Officially it is just a square and marketplace in the old city, but Jemaa el-Fnaa has functioned for centuries as Marrakesh's real centre of gravity, the one patch of ground locals and visitors have always shared. Every alley in the medina seems to lead here eventually, and it has never lost that job.
_facts: Square and market place in the medina (old city) of Marrakesh
Remains the main square of Marrakesh, used by locals and tourists

s: The hotel that hosted half of 20th-century fame
w: Mamounia means 'safe haven' in Arabic, and for a century that is what this hotel opposite the Kutubiyya Mosque has offered a bewildering guest list: Churchill, de Gaulle, Chaplin, Warhol, Mandela and Paul McCartney all passed through its gardens. Widely named the best hotel on Earth, it never shook the habit.
_facts: Five-star hotel opposite the Kutubiyya Mosque, opened as one of the world's most acclaimed hotels
Name means 'safe haven' or 'reservoir' in Arabic
Notable guests: Charles de Gaulle, Winston Churchill, FDR, Nelson Mandela, Charlie Chaplin, Paul McCartney, Andy Warhol, Marlene Dietrich, Gary Cooper, Yves Saint Laurent

n: Amal Women's Training Center and Moroccan Restaurant
s: A restaurant with a second purpose behind every plate
w: Since 2012, this nonprofit kitchen has trained disadvantaged Marrakshi women in professional cooking, thirty to forty of them a year, over four to six months, most walking into real jobs afterward. Founded by Nora Belahcen Fitzgerald, it serves Moroccan and international food to fund the training behind it.
_facts: Non-profit organisation training disadvantaged women in Moroccan and international cooking
Established 2012 by Nora Belahcen Fitzgerald
30-40 women complete 4-6 months of training each year, often leading to employment

s: The last Marinid monument standing in Marrakesh
w: The Marinids ruled Marrakesh for a stretch of the 14th century, yet almost nothing of their building work survives here except this mosque, the only major Marinid-era monument left standing in the city. Its finely decorated minaret is reason enough to track it down in the medina's backstreets.
_facts: 14th-century mosque in the historic medina of Marrakesh
Only major surviving Marinid-era monument in Marrakesh
Notable for its fine minaret

s: A mosque named after a rat-catching cat
w: The story goes that the founder's cat was enlisted to clear a vizier's house of rats, and the mosque his reward paid for has carried the name since. Founded by a student of Sufi saint Abu al-Abbas as-Sabti, rebuilt under the Marinids in the 14th century, it keeps a small, richly decorated minaret as its legacy.
_facts: Also known as the Mosque of the Cat, in the Ksour neighbourhood on Souk Laksour near Bab Ftouh
Founded by a student of 12th-century Sufi saint Abu al-Abbas as-Sabti
Name derives from a story in which the founder's cat cleared rats from a vizier's house
Renovated in the 14th century under the Marinid Sultanate; notable for its small, richly decorated minaret

s: The sultan's mosque, built into his own citadel
w: Raised in the late 18th century by the Alaouite sultan Muhammad ibn Abdallah, this mosque is stitched directly into the walls of the Kasbah and the Dar al-Makhzen royal palace. A place of worship that has always kept close company with power, rather than sitting apart from it.
_facts: Mosque attached to the Kasbah (citadel) and the Royal Palace (Dar al-Makhzen)
Built in the late 18th century by the Alawi sultan Muhammad ibn Abdallah

s: The quieter of two gates into the old citadel
w: Overshadowed by its more famous neighbour Bab Agnaou just to the north, Bab Ksiba does the same job with less fanfare: guarding an entrance into the Kasbah, the citadel quarter tucked into the southern end of Marrakesh's medina, itself a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
_facts: City gate in Marrakesh, serving with Bab Agnaou as an entrance to the Kasbah district
Kasbah sits in the southern part of the medina, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

s: The medina's main gate to the northwest
w: One of the medina's principal gates, marking the northwestern edge of Marrakesh's walled old city. Function over flourish: like the other Bab gates ringing the medina, it has spent centuries simply doing its job, letting the city in and out.
_facts: Main northwestern gate of the medina (historic walled city) of Marrakesh
